questions.prompt: What does the loop gain \(T\) of a feedback system measure?
options: The gain from the input to the output: \(G/(1+Gf)\)
The forward gain \(G\) alone
The gain of the feedback network alone, \(f\)
The gain once around the loop (cut the loop, inject a signal, and see what comes back): \(T=G\,f\)
questions.explanation:
Break the loop, apply a test signal at the break, and follow it through \(G\) and then \(f\): what returns is \(T=G\,f\). It is the quantity that decides how strongly the feedback acts.
• \(G/(1+T)\) is the closed-loop gain.
• \(G\) and \(f\) alone are only two of the factors in \(T\).

questions.prompt: Which condition makes the closed-loop gain \(G/(1+T)\) depend almost only on the feedback network, \(\approx 1/f\)?
options: The forward gain \(G\) must be small
The feedback factor \(f\) must equal 1
The LOOP gain must be large, \(T=Gf\gg1\)
\(G\gg1\) alone is enough, whatever \(f\) is
questions.explanation:
\(\dfrac{G}{1+T}\to\dfrac{G}{T}=\dfrac1f\) only when \(T\gg1\).
The last option is the subtle trap: a huge \(G\) paired with a tiny \(f\) can still give \(T\) near 1 (for example \(G=100\) and \(f=0.005\) gives \(T=0.5\)), and then the gain is NOT \(1/f\). It is important for \(T\) to be large, not just \(G\).

questions.prompt: A feedback loop has forward gain \(G=500\) and feedback gain \(f=0.04\). What is its loop gain \(T\)?
questions.explanation:
\(T=Gf=500\times0.04=20\): the gain a signal picks up going once around the loop. The closed-loop gain is then \(G/(1+T)=23.8\), close to \(1/f=25\).
• 500 is the forward gain alone.
• 25 is \(1/f\), the ideal closed-loop gain.
• 12500 divides by f instead of multiplying.

questions.prompt: A unity-feedback loop (\(f=1\)) must track a constant input with an error of at most 1% (\(e/x\le0.01\)). What is the minimum forward gain G?
questions.explanation:
\(e/x=1/(1+T)\) with \(T=G\). Setting \(1/(1+G)=0.01\) gives \(G=99\). The rule '1% error needs a loop gain of about 100' is the same result rounded.
• 100 is the rounded rule of thumb, slightly more than needed.
• 0.99 confuses the error with the output fraction.

questions.prompt: A disturbance (for example distortion) added at the forward block's output is reduced by feedback. If the input is adjusted so that the output signal has the same amplitude as without feedback, by what factor is the output disturbance reduced?
options: It is not reduced; feedback only changes the gain
questions.explanation:
A disturbance \(s_{noise}\) added at the output appears at the output as \(\dfrac{s_{noise}}{1+T}\), so for the same signal level the disturbance is \(1+T\) times smaller. The loop notices any unwanted output change as an error and corrects it.
• Gain \(G\) is the forward gain, not the loop's rejection factor.
• Saying nothing changes ignores Eq. 17.13.

questions.prompt: With a loop gain of \(T=200\), what is the fractional gain error \(\dfrac{1/f-G_{closed}}{1/f}\) of the closed-loop system, in percent?
questions.explanation:
\(G_{closed}=\dfrac{G}{1+T}\) and \(1/f=G/T\), so \(\dfrac{G_{closed}}{1/f}=\dfrac{T}{1+T}\) and the error is \(1-\dfrac{T}{1+T}=\dfrac{1}{1+T}=\dfrac{1}{201}=0.4975\%\).
Rule of thumb: the percent error is about \(100/T\).

questions.prompt: A system without feedback has output \(G\,s_{in}+s_{noise}\). With feedback the output is \(\dfrac{G}{1+T}s_{in}+\dfrac{1}{1+T}s_{noise}\), with \(T=100\). You apply the SAME input amplitude in both cases. What happens to the signal-to-noise ratio at the output?
options: Unchanged: the signal AND the noise are both reduced by \(1+T\). You only gain if you raise the input to restore the output level
Improves by a factor of 101, since the noise is divided by 101
Gets worse by a factor of 101, since the gain fell by 101
Improves by a factor of 100, since \(T=100\)
questions.explanation:
With the same input, the output signal falls by \(1+T\) (the closed-loop gain \(G/(1+T)\) is lower) and the output noise also falls by \(1+T\), so the ratio \(\dfrac{G\,s_{in}}{s_{noise}}\) is unchanged.
The benefit appears when you compare at equal OUTPUT level: the input must be \(1+T\) times larger, and the noise injected at the output is still \(1+T\) times smaller, so the SNR improves by \(1+T\) (if the input signal can be raised for free).
• 'Improves by 101' is only right when the output amplitude is held fixed; here the input is fixed.

questions.prompt: To measure the loop gain, set the input \(x=0\), break the loop at the input of G, inject a test signal \(v_t\) there, and measure the signal \(v_r\) that comes back around the loop to the break point. How is T defined?
options: \(T=v_r/v_t\), which is negative for negative feedback
\(T=-v_r/v_t\); the minus sign accounts for the subtraction at the summing junction, so \(T=Gf\) is positive for negative feedback
questions.explanation:
Going around the loop, \(v_t\) is multiplied by G, then by f, then by \(-1\) at the summing junction: \(v_r=-Gfv_t\), so \(-v_r/v_t=Gf=T\). With this sign convention, a positive T means negative feedback, and \(T=-1\) is the oscillation condition.
• Without the minus sign, negative feedback would give a negative T and the usual \(1+T\) formulas would break.
• The inverse ratio and the difference are not gains.

questions.prompt: A feedback loop has \(f=0.1\). Its forward gain G rises by 25%, from 400 to 500. By what percentage does the closed-loop gain change?
questions.explanation:
\(400/41=9.756\) and \(500/51=9.804\), a change of 0.49%. Feedback divides the 25% change by roughly the loop gain plus one: \(25\%/41\approx0.6\%\) for small changes; for a change this large the exact ratio gives 0.49%.
• 25% is the open-loop change.
• 2.5% divides by 10 instead of \(1+T\).

questions.prompt: Preview of gain-bandwidth. A loop has \(T(jf)=\dfrac{2000}{1+jf/(100\ \mathrm{Hz})}\). At what frequency does \(|T|\) fall to 1? Give the exact value in kHz.
questions.explanation:
Set \(|T|=1\): \(\dfrac{2000}{\sqrt{1+(f/100)^2}}=1\Rightarrow f=100\sqrt{2000^2-1}=200000\ \mathrm{Hz}\approx200\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
Equivalent shortcut: gain × frequency stays near \(2000\times100\ \mathrm{Hz}=200\ \mathrm{kHz}\) on the \(-20\ \mathrm{dB/decade}\) slope. This 'unity-loop-gain frequency' sets the bandwidth in the next skills.

questions.prompt: Preview of dynamic errors. The loop gain of a system is \(T(j\omega)=\dfrac{T_0}{1+j\omega/\omega_p}\). The closed-loop gain error is about \(1/|1+T|\). As the signal frequency rises well above \(\omega_p\), what happens to the gain error?
options: It stays constant at \(1/(1+T_0)\)
It shrinks, because high frequencies are attenuated more
It grows, because \(|T|\) falls with frequency, so there is less loop gain to correct errors
It becomes exactly zero once \(|T|<1\)
questions.explanation:
The error is controlled by the available loop gain AT the signal frequency. Above \(\omega_p\), \(|T|\approx T_0\omega_p/\omega\) drops by 20 dB per decade, so the error \(\approx 1/|T|\) rises by 20 dB per decade, until \(|T|\approx1\) where the feedback has essentially no effect.
• It is constant only at low frequency.
• At \(|T|<1\) the loop has almost no authority: the error is large, not zero.

questions.prompt: Preview of stability. At some frequency a loop picks up so much phase lag that the loop gain is \(T=-0.8\) (magnitude 0.8, phase \(-180^\circ\)), so the feedback ADDS to the input instead of subtracting. By what factor is the closed-loop gain \(\dfrac{G}{1+T}\) larger than the forward gain \(G\) at that frequency?
questions.explanation:
\(\dfrac{G_{closed}}{G}=\dfrac{1}{1+T}=\dfrac{1}{1+(-0.8)}=\dfrac{1}{0.2}=5\).
So the response has a 5× peak at that frequency, even though \(|T|<1\). If \(T\) reached \(-1\) the denominator would vanish: the closed loop would produce output with no input at all, which is oscillation. That is why the stability skill asks how far \(T\) stays from \(-1\) when \(|T|=1\).
